questions.stem: An acquirer's host reads DE 43 as a fixed field of 40 characters. A new kiosk gateway now sends DE 43 as a variable field, and leaves DE 60 as it always was. The host's log now says it cannot unpack DE 60. Where is the fault?

options.text: In DE 60, since the host found too few length digits in front of that field's value
options.says: the host looked for DE 60's length in the wrong place because DE 43 had shifted everything; DE 60 is unchanged

options.text: In DE 43, since the host took the gateway's length digits as name and so misread the later fields
options.says: nothing marks where a field ends but the receiver's table, so one field in the wrong format shifts every later field and the error names a later one

options.text: In DE 60, since the gateway wrote too few length digits in front of that field's value
options.says: the gateway did not change DE 60; the host read its length digits from the wrong place because DE 43 had shifted everything

options.text: In DE 43, since the host stopped at the end of the gateway's short name and so misread the later fields
options.says: the host does not stop at the end of the name: it takes all 40 characters, which here include the gateway's length digits and part of the next field

origin.section: 3.1. A Field's Format Is All the Receiver Has to Find Where It Ends

questions.stem: A developer, unsure how amounts are written, calls set(4, "12.50") for a sale of 12.50 and packs the message with iso87ascii.xml. What happens?

options.text: The message is not packed, since DE 4 is numeric and the value holds a character that is not a digit
options.says: jPOS checks the length of a value, not its characters, so the dot is accepted

options.text: The message is not packed, since a value for DE 4 must be given with all twelve digits
options.says: a short value is padded with zeros on the left; only a value that is too long is refused

options.text: The message goes out with 000000012.50 in DE 4, since the value is padded to twelve characters as it is
options.says: jPOS pads a short value and checks nothing but its length, so the dot travels to the host

options.text: The message goes out with 000000001250 in DE 4, since the dot is dropped as the value is padded
options.says: the packager does not interpret the value; it pads what it was given, dot included

origin.section: 3.2. A Short Value Is Padded, a Long One Is Refused, and Nothing Else Is Checked

questions.stem: A link packs DE 2 in BCD with a one-byte length prefix. A card has a 15-digit PAN. What does the sender put on the wire for DE 2?

options.text: The prefix counts digits, and the 15 digits behind it fill 8 bytes
options.says: a BCD prefix counts digits, two digits share a byte, and the spare half-byte is filled

options.text: The prefix counts bytes, and the 15 digits behind it fill 8 bytes
options.says: a BCD prefix counts digits, not bytes; a peer that reads it as bytes misreads the field and everything after it

options.text: The prefix counts digits, and the 15 digits behind it fill 15 bytes
options.says: one byte per digit is ASCII or EBCDIC; BCD packs two digits into each byte

options.text: The prefix counts bytes, and the 15 digits behind it fill 15 bytes
options.says: BCD packs two digits into each byte, and its prefix counts digits, not bytes

origin.section: 3.3. The Packager Decides the Bytes, So Both Peers Need the Same One

questions.stem: A terminal application builds Track 2 as 4111111111111111D2812101 and the link packs DE 35 with a BCD field packager. What does the issuer get when it unpacks DE 35?

options.text: The track as the terminal built it, since BCD has a half-byte value for the letter D
options.says: jPOS's BCD packager maps the character = to the half-byte D; a D character is packed as a digit

options.text: The track with = in place of D, since the packager turns one separator form into the other
options.says: only = is turned into the half-byte D and back; a D set in the message is not recognised as the separator

options.text: A run of digits with a 4 in place of the separator, since the letter D is packed as a digit
options.says: the BCD packager packs D as 4, so the separator is gone and the PAN can no longer be found

options.text: A run of digits one shorter than the track, since the packager drops each character that is not a digit
options.says: nothing is dropped: the D becomes the digit 4, so the track keeps its length and loses its separator

origin.section: 3.4. A Field's Type Decides How You Read Its Value

questions.stem: A team adds one check for every message it receives: reject anything without DE 2, DE 4 and DE 11. The network sends its first 0800 echo test of the day. What does the check do?

options.text: It rejects the echo, since a network message carries no card number and no amount
options.says: which fields are present depends on the MTI; an 0800 echo carries DE 7, DE 11 and DE 70

options.text: It rejects the echo, since a network message carries its trace number in DE 70 instead
options.says: an 0800 echo carries its STAN in DE 11; it fails the check because it has no DE 2 and no DE 4

options.text: It lets the echo through, since a network message carries a card number and amount of zero
options.says: an 0800 echo carries no DE 2 and no DE 4 at all, only DE 7, DE 11 and DE 70

options.text: It lets the echo through, since getString returns zeros for a field that was not sent
options.says: getString returns null for an absent field, and hasField is false

origin.section: 3.5. Which Fields Must Be Present Depends on the MTI and the Network
